title: N-D-R

cards: "I'll bring the dessert on Friday, bli neder." Listen around some Jewish tables and you'll hear those two words tacked onto ordinary promises. Bli neder: without a vow.
It sounds like a hedge, a way of getting out of the cake. It's the opposite. It comes from taking a vow so seriously that you don't want a casual promise about dessert to become one by accident.

teach.h: DO ALL THAT PROCEEDETH OUT OF HIS MOUTH.
teach.b: N-D-R. Nun, dalet, resh. Neder: a vow, a promise made before God.
First, the weight of a word. The Torah says that when someone vows a vow, "he shall not break his word, he shall do according to all that proceedeth out of his mouth."
What comes out of your mouth becomes something you owe. Second, the advice.

teach.h: BETTER NOT TO VOW THAN NOT TO PAY.
teach.b: Ecclesiastes, Kohelet, the Gatherer from a few days ago, says it plainly: "Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay." Not a ban on vows. A warning about making them cheap.
That's where bli neder comes from: a habit of guarding the word. Third, the night the vows are spoken about.

Yom Kippur evening opens with Kol Nidre, all vows, from this root: a legal formula, sung slowly, that asks for release from vows a person can't keep. It's been argued over and explained in more than one way.

Some read it as a mercy for the person who promised too much. Some hear a whole community admitting how often words outrun lives. Either way, Yom Kippur night begins not with a hymn but with the subject of promises.
And yesterday's word is the neighbor here.

teach.h: NEDAVAH HANDED OVER, NEDER TAKEN ON.
teach.b: The rabbis set the two side by side: a nedavah is a gift you hand over, a neder is a promise you take on. One letter apart, and both start with a willing heart.

teach.h: A VOW FOLLOWS YOU OUT THE DOOR.
teach.b: But a vow follows you out the door.

how: Some Jews add bli neder, 'without a vow', to everyday promises so they won't become binding vows, and the evening service of Yom Kippur begins with Kol Nidre, a formula about the release of vows.

games.q: a friend asks if you'll bring dessert on Friday. you plan to, but you're careful with your word. what do some Jews add?
games.why: bli neder: a promise kept as a promise, without becoming a vow. taking vows seriously means not making them by accident.

practice: Bring to mind a promise that's still open, not a grand one: I'll call you back, I'll be there Saturday.

Notice the ones that slipped without punishing yourself, then choose one you can actually keep and picture it done, your word and your day lining up again. If you pray, you can bring that promise into your prayer.
